## Two weeks of "tolerance," never defined {.section-title}

We built explanations of a forum where "participants became more tolerant."

We never once asked: **what do we mean by tolerance?**

**Running exercise: What is social media?** Give a one-sentence definition. Name one clear example and one borderline case.

::: notes
Opening, including the title slide. Put the forum sentence back on the board exactly as Week 2 used it: "Forum participants became more tolerant." Ask the class: over two full seminars, did we ever pin down what tolerance *is*? Take two or three quick answers. Expected responses will gesture at willingness to extend a right, or absence of hostility, or something similar — all plausible, none identical, none stated as an explicit definition at the time.

The point is not that Week 2 made a mistake. Description and explanation can proceed for a while on a shared, fuzzy sense of a term. The point is that this only works until it doesn't: the moment two people mean different things by "tolerance," every claim about it — descriptive or causal — becomes ambiguous in a way neither the descriptive-target machinery nor the covering-law/mechanism machinery from Weeks 1–2 can rescue. Concepts are prior to both.

Tell the class directly what today accomplishes: Weeks 1–2 asked what counts as an explanation once you already have a target and a set of variables. Week 3 asks where the target and the variables come from in the first place — how a fuzzy idea like "tolerance" becomes a usable concept at all. This is not a detour from explanation; it is what has to happen before explanation can start.

Social media application (instructor exercise): Begin with an individual provisional definition, then collect two contrasting definitions aloud. Keep a shared board record of the working definition, defining attributes, included cases, excluded cases, and unresolved cases. Students revise the same definition throughout the seminar. This is a classroom application of the readings, not a definition supplied by any of the authors. Use these revisits in place of optional extra examples.

Source: Week 2 forum example, revisited. Course framing.
:::

## Bad concepts break description and causation alike

**Descriptive claim:** "Participants became more tolerant." Tolerant of *what*, exactly?

**Causal claim:** "Education increases tolerance." Which of several different things called "tolerance"?

::: key-line
A vague concept doesn't just weaken an explanation — it can make it impossible to state.
:::

::: project-caption
This isn't hypothetical: it's the actual state of "affective polarization" research. See Druckman & Levendusky (2019), *Public Opinion Quarterly*.
:::

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 3–6 minutes.

Land the pivot concretely using both halves of Weeks 1–2. First, the *explanandum* problem: Hirschman's stylized fact and Elster's "fact to be established" both presuppose that we already know what the fact is a fact about. If "tolerance" bundles three different things — willingness to let a disliked group speak, absence of hostile feeling, and public compliance with a norm — then "tolerance rose" isn't one descriptive claim, it's an ambiguous compression of at least three, and we can't even agree on what needs to be explained.

Second, the *causal-variable* problem: Hedström's variable concepts and Gerring's causal-utility criterion (previewed, not yet named) both require a variable clean enough to serve as one side of a causal claim. "Education increases tolerance" is not testable until "tolerance" picks out one specific, measurable thing — otherwise a study confirming the claim under one operationalization and a study refuting it under another are not actually in disagreement; they were never talking about the same variable.

Make the point land as a live, real methodological problem, not just a classroom hypothetical: Druckman and Levendusky (2019), "What Do We Measure When We Measure Affective Polarization?" (*Public Opinion Quarterly* 83(1): 114–122), is a direct, published version of exactly this diagnosis, in a field this course covers. The field's standard measure of "affective polarization" is the feeling-thermometer difference: how much colder people rate the opposing party than their own. Druckman and Levendusky show this single number bundles together several conceptually distinct things that can move independently — dislike of ordinary out-party *people* versus dislike of party *elites*; polarization driven by policy disagreement versus polarization that persists even holding policy views constant; and a general negativity/social-desirability bias that inflates in-group warmth ratings for reasons unrelated to the out-party at all. Two studies can both report "affective polarization increased" using the identical thermometer-difference measure while capturing substantively different underlying phenomena — the same mega-concept problem as "tolerance," now in a published, widely cited literature rather than a classroom example.

Ask the class to connect this explicitly to the causal-variable problem just stated: if a researcher claims "exposure to X increases affective polarization," which of Druckman and Levendusky's several bundled components is actually the dependent variable? A finding that X increases elite-directed animus and a finding that X leaves people-directed animus unchanged are not in tension — they may both be true — but a single thermometer-difference number cannot tell them apart, and two papers using "the same" measure may not be talking about the same variable at all. This is precisely why explication is not academic housekeeping: an entire literature can accumulate contradictory-looking findings that are actually just measuring different things under one label.

State the thesis for today plainly: a concept is not a free byproduct of having an idea. It has to be built, and it can be built well or badly. Today gives two complementary toolkits for building it well — Gerring's criteria for what makes a concept *good*, and McLeod & Pan's process for how you actually *construct* one — and one live example, Molina et al.'s explication of "fake news," where we watch both toolkits used for real.

Source: Course framing, building on Elster pp. 15–20 and Hedström pp. 11–14 (Week 2). Druckman, James N., and Matthew S. Levendusky. 2019. "What Do We Measure When We Measure Affective Polarization?" *Public Opinion Quarterly* 83(1): 114–122.
:::

## A concept is not the same thing as a word

**Sentence:** "A competent journalist writes clearly."

Five words. **Four concepts:** journalist, competence, writing, clarity.

::: key-line
"A," "the," and other function words are linguistic terms, not concepts.
:::

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 6–9 minutes.

Introduce McLeod & Pan's foundational distinction. A *linguistic term* is the smallest unit in a sentence — every word counts. A *concept* is a basic unit of meaning: a single word or a phrase that denotes some real-world referent (a person, a behavior, a quality, a relationship). Not every linguistic term is a concept — articles and prepositions carry no independent referent — and one concept can take more than one word ("television violence viewing" is a single concept expressed in three words).

Walk the class through the example sentence live: ask them to name the concepts, not the words. If someone says "a" is a concept, ask what real-world thing it refers to; there isn't one. This distinction matters immediately for today's whole-class exercises: when we ask "what's the concept here," we are asking about the idea being pointed at, not parsing grammar.

Source: McLeod & Pan, pp. 14–17.
:::

## McLeod & Pan's six types of concepts

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Singular** | A particular named person, place, or thing | “The September 9 forum” |
| **Class** | Objects grouped by shared attributes | Forums, journalists |
| **Relational** | A connection between concepts | “Positively related to,” “causes” |
| **Variable** | An attribute that varies among objects in a class | Tolerance, competence |
| **Process** | A way things change | Priming, institutionalization |
| **Mega-concept** | Several concepts, often unspecified, bundled together | Democracy, development, social media |

Process concepts are a special subcategory of mega-concepts (p. 17).

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 9–12 minutes.

Present this as Gerring's version of exactly the same structure McLeod & Pan just gave us, under different names. Term = the linguistic label (a linguistic term, in McLeod & Pan's sense). Intension = the conceptual definition — the attributes doing the defining work. Indicator = the operational definition — how we'd actually go find it in the world. Extension = the set of real things that end up qualifying once the intension and indicators are fixed.

Make the mutual-adjustment point explicit and concrete: if we tighten the intension of "democracy" by adding "civil liberties" as a second required attribute alongside "contested elections," some countries that used to qualify (extension) now fall out, and we may need new indicators to detect civil liberties specifically. Change any one corner, and the concept moves as a whole — this is why Gerring insists concept formation has to be viewed holistically rather than as fixing definitions in isolation.

Flag, without dwelling, that this four-part structure explains why "operationalization" (Gerring's seventh, deferred criterion; McLeod & Pan's fifth Chaffee step) keeps reappearing all class: it's not a separate later task bolted onto conceptualization, it's one of the four elements that was always part of the concept's structure from the start.

Source: Gerring, pp. 114–115.
:::

## Whole-class: name the type

Using our own Week 2 vocabulary:

1.  "Tolerance" — what type of concept?
2.  "The September 9 forum" — what type?
3.  "Positively related to" — what type?
4.  "Television" — what type? (Hold that thought.)

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 12–14 minutes.

Quick cold-call check, one answer per item, moving fast. Expected: (1) tolerance is a *variable* concept — an attribute along which people differ in degree. (2) The September 9 forum is a *singular* concept — one particular, named event; "forums in general" would instead be a *class* concept. (3) "Positively related to" is a *relational* concept — it connects two other concepts (e.g., education and tolerance) without itself denoting a person, place, or attribute. (4) "Television" is the trap: students will likely say *class* concept (a category of devices or content), and that's defensible, but flag that in a research claim like "television is harmful," it's functioning as an ill-specified *variable* — or worse, several different unspecified variables bundled together. Don't resolve this fully; it's the hook into the next segment.

If time allows, ask for one volunteered example from a student's own project and classify it live. Keep this to one example; the exit prompt returns to personal projects at the end of class.

Source: Whole-class application of McLeod & Pan's typology (pp. 14–17) to Week 2 material.
:::

## Gerring's Figure 5.1: tightening a definition shrinks its reach

**Necessary-condition attributes:** more intension → less extension.

Democracy = "free and fair elections" *and* "civil liberties"?

Fewer countries qualify than under "free and fair elections" alone.

::: key-line
Adding requirements can only narrow — never widen — who counts, when each requirement is necessary.
:::

::: notes
Set up the tradeoff verbally before showing the figure on the next slide. Ask the class to predict, before any diagram appears, what happens to the set of countries counted as democracies if "civil liberties" is added as a second required attribute alongside "free and fair elections." Take one or two guesses, then move to the figure to confirm the mechanism visually.

Source: Gerring, pp. 121–123.
:::

## Gerring's Figure 5.1: intension and extension

![](assets/gerring-figure5.1-intension-extension.png){fig-alt="Gerring's Figure 5.1: a chart plotting intension (number of attributes) against extension (number of referents), with a solid line showing an inverse relationship for necessary-condition attributes and a dashed line showing a direct relationship for sufficient-condition attributes." fig-align="center" width="1050" height="586"}

**Adding necessary attributes narrows membership.** Requiring elections *and* civil liberties admits fewer countries, or the same number.

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 14–17 minutes.

Flag the flip side briefly, without spending much time: if attributes are instead treated as ***sufficient*** conditions (any one alone is enough to qualify — direct popular rule *or* indirect popular rule *or* deliberative rule, each independently sufficient), then adding attributes can only widen the extension, the opposite direction. Gerring notes this sufficient-condition case is much rarer in practice than the necessary-condition case; most social-science attributes are understood as necessary, necessary-and-sufficient, or as a matter of degree (additive/continuous), all of which behave like the necessary-condition case.

Do not let this become a logic-notation exercise. The payoff is entirely practical: whenever a definition changes and someone reacts "wait, that changes who counts," this tradeoff is exactly why — and it is the mechanism behind a concept-formation failure we are about to name in Gerring's criteria.

Source: Gerring, pp. 121–123, Figure 5.1.
:::

## Exercise: predict the tradeoff, on our own definition

Our working definition so far: *social media = a platform for publishing user-generated content to others.*

Now add a second necessary condition: *...and organizes what users see via an algorithmic feed.*

1.  Does the set of qualifying platforms on our board grow, shrink, or stay the same?
2.  Name one item from our board list that would now *drop out*.
3.  Is "algorithmic feed" being treated as necessary, or as a matter of degree?

::: notes
Fast, cold-call, no small groups. Bring back the actual board list from the opening exercise — clear examples and borderline cases the class already named for "social media" — and apply the tradeoff to it directly rather than to a fresh example. Expected answer to (1): shrink, or stay the same at best; reinforce the mechanism from the previous slide rather than re-deriving it.

For (2), push the class to use their own board items. Plain email, a group text thread, or a static personal blog are likely candidates to drop out — user-generated content, but no algorithmic feed organizing what anyone sees. A borderline case like Wikipedia or a LinkedIn feed is exactly the kind of case worth debating live: does a lightly-ranked or mostly-chronological feed count as "algorithmic" enough? Let the disagreement run for a moment before moving on — the point is that the board's own borderline cases are precisely where this kind of attribute-adding is felt, not resolved by fiat.

For (3), most students will say "matter of degree" once pressed — algorithmic curation ranges from simple chronological ranking to fully personalized machine-learned feeds, which is exactly the additive/continuous case Gerring says produces the same narrowing direction as a strict necessary condition, just via a shrinking *fit* rather than a sharp in/out cut.

Transition: "We now have the machinery — term, intension, indicator, extension, and how tightening intension moves extension. Gerring uses this machinery to state six criteria for judging whether a concept is any good. We're going to work them out by diagnosis: I'll show you a bad example first, and you tell me what's wrong before I tell you the criterion's name."

Source: Whole-class application of Gerring's Figure 5.1 logic to the running social-media exercise.
:::

## Diagnose: "Social media is harmful to the political process."

Sounds like a claim. Is it testable?

1.  What, precisely, is "social media"?
2.  What, precisely, is "harmful"?
3.  Harmful to *what* — voters? officials? institutions?

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 19–22 minutes.

“Social media” could refer to time spent scrolling that displaces other activities; exposure to political information; encountering hostile or misleading posts; participation in political discussion; or politicians adapting their messages to attract engagement. Each interpretation points to a different activity, unit, comparison, and research design. These are possible meanings and hypotheses, not established effects. Ask students to select one interpretation and say what would have to vary for the claim to become testable.

"Harmful to the political process" is even worse off: it names no dimension at all. Turnout? Trust in institutions? Knowledge of issues? Quality of deliberation? Each is a legitimate variable concept; the sentence picks none of them.

The diagnosis: "social media" and "the political process" are each *mega-concepts* — compound tangles of unspecified variable concepts — masquerading as single, already-operationalizable variables. This is the same disease "tolerance" has in our forum example, just easier to see from the outside.

Source: Classroom adaptation of McLeod & Pan’s meaning-analysis example, pp. 19–21. Social media scenarios are instructor illustrations.
:::

## Four standards a scientific concept has to meet

| Standard                 | What it demands                             |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Abstractness**         | Applies beyond one person, place, or moment |
| **Clarity of meaning**   | Says what it does and doesn't include       |
| **Operationalizability** | Can be turned into an observation procedure |
| **Precision**            | Others can understand and evaluate it       |

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 22–24 minutes.

Quickly name McLeod & Pan's four standards and diagnose "television" against them, closing the loop from the previous slide. It is plenty abstract — it applies across many times, places, and studies. It fails clarity of meaning outright: as the last slide showed, it doesn't tell us which of five different things it means. Operationalizability is oddly not the bottleneck here — all five interpretations are individually measurable — the bottleneck is that we haven't chosen among them. Precision, which McLeod & Pan treat as the broadest standard (can this be communicated to other scientists and to nonscientists alike?), is unreachable until clarity of meaning is fixed first.

Note the built-in tension the reading flags: abstractness and operationalizability pull against each other — the more abstract a concept, the harder it is to operationalize; the more easily operationalized, the more it risks losing abstractness (a single-item, single-context measure). Concept explication is the discipline for holding both at once, which is exactly what the rest of today builds toward.

Social media application (instructor exercise): Ask students to rewrite one vague phrase and propose an observation that could help classify a borderline service. Distinguish a clearer definition from a merely longer one.

Source: McLeod & Pan, pp. 18–19.
:::

## Seven everyday ways people define concepts (part 1)

| Approach | Example | Weakness |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| By examples | "Social media? Discussion forums, photo-sharing apps..." | |
| By exclusion | "Social media is not email or a static website" |  |
| Comparing subsets | "Opinion leaders vs. everyone else" |  |
| By procedure | "IQ is a score on this test" |  |

**Our definition:** Does listing familiar platforms tell us what makes a new service social media?

::: notes
Frame all four as useful starting points that cannot, individually, finish the work of defining a research concept. Each makes an idea concrete — by pointing to examples, exclusions, group differences, or a measurement procedure — but each also leaves the underlying meaning, and its reach beyond the immediate cases, unspecified. Walk through all four using the same running social-media example so the parallel is unmistakable.

**1. By examples: "Social media means discussion forums and photo-sharing apps."** This helps a listener recognize the kind of thing under discussion, and gives candidate cases for the extension. But what do these examples actually share that makes them social media? User-created content? Interaction? Public visibility? Connections among users? The list doesn't say which attributes are required, which are optional, or how to combine them into a membership rule. Ask: "A new website lets readers publish comments beneath news articles. Does it belong on the list, and why?" If a student can only name another familiar platform, they've extended the list without stating the rule. In Gerring's terms: examples illustrate the extension without specifying the intension.

**2. By exclusion: "Social media is not email or a static personal website."** The mirror image of the first approach, and no better off. Email is excluded because it isn't public; a static website is excluded because it isn't interactive — two different reasons, neither of which tells us what the *included* cases share. A rule built entirely from what something *isn't* can correctly exclude everything on a list of non-examples while still leaving the actual membership rule for what's left completely unstated. Ask: does excluding email and a personal blog tell us whether a subscription newsletter with an open comment section belongs?

**3. Comparing subsets: "Opinion leaders are more informed and more consulted than everyone else."** Useful for noticing that members of a class differ from one another — but it presupposes, rather than states, the underlying general variable driving that difference. Applied here: calling some users "power users" and others "casual users" describes a difference in degree without ever naming which single attribute — posting frequency? follower count? engagement rate? — actually constitutes it. The comparison is real; the variable behind it is left implicit.

**4. By procedure: "IQ is whatever this test measures."** For social media: "A platform counts as social media if it appears on this analytics firm's tracked list." This buys apparent precision and replicability — but risks the *reification fallacy* we'll name properly with Molina et al. later: treating the measurement procedure as though it settles what the concept itself means. If the tracked-platforms list is wrong, outdated, or contested, procedure alone gives no independent way to say so, because the procedure and the concept have been silently identified with each other.

Ask the class: "Which of these four did we just unknowingly use on 'social media is harmful to the political process' a few slides ago?" Likely answer: by examples and by procedure — treating "social media" as self-evidently whatever a familiar handful of platforms are, without asking which dimension of use actually matters for the claim.

Source: McLeod & Pan, Table 2.2 and pp. 21–26. Opinion leadership and IQ are examples from the reading; social media examples and classroom questions are instructor adaptations.
:::

## Seven everyday ways people define concepts (part 2)

| Approach       | Example                                         | Weakness |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| By analogy     | "A frame is like a window on the world"         |  |
| By function    | "Fear appeal = arouses emotional reaction"      |  |
| By antecedents | "Dissonance = tension from conflicting beliefs" |  |

::: key-line
Concept explication is the eighth approach — it doesn't discard these seven, it disciplines them.
:::

::: notes
**5. By analogy: "Social media is a public square" / "a frame is like a window on the world."** Drawing a comparison to something familiar illuminates fast — a public square suggests open, many-to-many communication, which is genuinely part of what social media is. But an analogy imports whatever the source domain happens to highlight while silently hiding what it doesn't: a public square doesn't have an algorithm deciding who hears whom, doesn't collect and sell data on everyone present, and doesn't have a private company setting the rules of entry. McLeod & Pan point to the framing literature's own "fractured paradigm" problem as a case where analogy-based definitions (a frame as a "window," a "picture frame," a "story line") never converged on a shared meaning, precisely because each analogy licensed a different, only partly overlapping set of implications.

**6. By function: "Fear appeal = a message that arouses an emotional reaction."** Defining a concept by the effect it produces is useful for latent, hard-to-observe constructs — we can't directly see "fear appeal" in a message, but we can observe whether audiences react fearfully. The risk is circularity: if the *only* evidence that a message qualifies as a fear appeal is that it produced fear, the definition can't be used to predict or explain that same reaction without assuming what it's trying to establish. Applied to social media: calling a platform feature "addictive" because it's associated with heavy use defines the feature by the very outcome we might want to explain.

**7. By antecedents: "Dissonance is the tension that comes from holding conflicting beliefs."** The mirror-image move — defining a concept by its presumed cause rather than its effect. Same risk in reverse: if dissonance is identified only by the presence of conflicting beliefs, and conflicting beliefs are identified only by the dissonance they're presumed to cause, the two claims can prop each other up without either being independently testable. Walk through the trap concretely: a researcher observes someone who freely chose an option and now expresses a more favorable opinion of it than before, and explains this by saying "they experienced dissonance from holding conflicting beliefs about their choice." Pressed further — "how do we know they held conflicting beliefs in the first place?" — the only evidence on offer is the belief change itself, which is exactly the thing dissonance was invoked to explain. The antecedent and the outcome have been defined into each other, so the "explanation" can't fail: whatever the person does afterward can always be redescribed as proof that dissonance must have been present.

The fix runs the same way for both #6 and #7: find an indicator of the antecedent (or the function) that doesn't depend on already knowing the outcome it's meant to explain. For dissonance, that might be a self-reported measure of discomfort captured *before* the belief change is measured, or an experimentally manipulated condition (freely chosen vs. assigned) whose presence doesn't rely on the belief-change measure at all. Applied to social media: it's the identical trap to say a post "went viral because it was controversial" while defining "controversial" as nothing more than "the kind of content that goes viral" — controversy needs its own independent marker (coded disagreement in the replies, a polarized ratio of positive to negative reactions) measured separately from the virality it's supposed to explain.

State the punchline plainly: none of these seven is illegitimate — each is a real, common move, and Gerring's own "strategies" section later in class reuses some of this same logic. The problem is relying on only one, in isolation, without an integrating discipline. That discipline is McLeod & Pan's eighth approach: *concept explication* — analyzing a concept's meaning, describing its essential qualities, identifying its dimensions when it's complex, and prescribing how it connects to the empirical world. The rest of today is about what that discipline actually looks like, using Gerring's criteria for judging the result and McLeod & Pan's own six-step process for producing it.

Source: McLeod & Pan, Table 2.2 and pp. 24–26. Framing, fear appeal, and cognitive dissonance draw on the reading; the social media examples are instructor illustrations, not reported findings or validated definitions.
:::

# What makes for a "good" concept?

## Diagnose: "Democracy: a furry, four-legged animal." {.section-title}

What's wrong here — and how is it different from ordinary disagreement about democracy?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 29–31 minutes.

This is Gerring's own reductio, presented deliberately as an absurd case before the six criteria are named one by one, so the class has a shared benchmark for "obviously bad" against which every subsequent diagnosis can be measured. Ask: is this definition *false*? In one sense no — it's not that "furry, four-legged animal" misdescribes some real feature of democracies; it's that the definition has nothing to do with any established sense of the word at all. Distinguish this from a real scholarly disagreement (e.g., electoral vs. liberal definitions of democracy), where competing definitions still all resonate with *some* recognizable, shared sense of "rule by the people."

Let the class try to name what's broken before revealing the label. Likely answers: "it's not what anyone means by that word," "it's just made up," "it violates common usage." All of these are gesturing at the same thing.

Source: Gerring, p. 117.
:::

## Criterion 1: Resonance

**Bad:** "democracy: a furry, four-legged animal" — pure stipulation, zero shared usage.

**Good:** democracy as *"rule by the people"* — every competing definition still revolves around this core.

::: key-line
Resonance: how faithful is the concept to established usage?
:::

::: notes
Name the criterion: *resonance* — the degree to which a term or definition conforms to established usage rather than clashing with it. A purely stipulative definition, defined "on the authority of the author" alone with no tether to how the term is actually used, has zero resonance; at the limit (nonsense words) it isn't understood at all.

Contrast with the good case: "rule by the people" as democracy's core meaning has strong resonance precisely because virtually every rival scholarly definition — electoral, liberal, majoritarian, participatory, deliberative, egalitarian (we'll see this full taxonomy later) — still orbits this same core idea, even while disagreeing about what "rule by the people" cashes out to institutionally. Resonance doesn't require consensus on every detail; it requires that competing definitions are recognizably arguing about the same thing.

Flag the real methodological version of this failure, not just the cartoon one: jargon terms with no lay resonance ("vouchers," in Gerring's example) may achieve resonance within one specialist community while failing it for a broader audience — resonance is always relative to a specified audience, which is exactly what the next criterion, domain, is about.

Social media application (instructor exercise): Ask for one surprising inclusion or exclusion and whether the research purpose justifies departing from common usage.

Source: Gerring, pp. 116–117.
:::

## Diagnose: is this democracy definition universal?

A textbook defines democracy using only contemporary Western nation-state institutions: political parties, competitive elections, an independent judiciary.

Is this definition *wrong*?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 33–35 minutes.

Present the case neutrally and let the class debate before naming the criterion. Push back on an initial "yes, it's wrong" reaction: is it wrong, or is it simply *scoped* — built for one domain (contemporary nation-states in the Western tradition) and silently presented as if it covered every domain (ancient Athens' direct assemblies, local community governance, transnational advocacy coalitions, even — Gerring's own example — "democratic" modes of dress and comportment)?

Expected answer once pressed: the definition itself may be perfectly serviceable *within* its intended domain; the problem is failing to say what that domain is. A concept, like an argument, can only be evaluated once its domain of usage is understood — no social-science concept is truly universal, and pretending otherwise is the actual failure, not the narrowness itself.

Source: Gerring, pp. 118–120.
:::

## Criterion 2: Domain

Does our definition describe **modern representative states**, or democracy in other settings too?

| Setting | Democratic feature | Different institutional requirements |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Worker cooperative | Equal member voting rights and shared control | Political parties and a separate judiciary need not be internal institutions |
| Citizens’ assembly | Representative participation and deliberation | Members can be selected by lottery rather than competitive elections |
| Member-run association | Members directly vote on rules and budgets | No elected representatives required in this example |

**Domain:** Specify both the language community and the settings the concept covers.

**Social media:** Whose usage, which platforms, and what time period does your definition cover?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 35–37 minutes.

Name the criterion: *domain* — both the linguistic domain (which audiences must find this resonant: lay readers? policymakers? one academic subfield?) and the empirical (phenomenal) domain (which contexts the concept is meant to apply to: local communities, nation-states, transnational coalitions, or, per Gerring's own deliberately broad example, modes of dress and comportment).

The good example is Gerring's own practice, not a hypothetical: rather than offering one all-purpose definition of democracy, he explicitly considers four different empirical domains and notes that some attributes (e.g., "contestation") clearly apply to nation-states but barely at all to modes of dress. The many rival definitions of democracy in circulation are not wrong on this view — they are *partial*, each staking out a different domain, and the failure is only in presenting a partial definition as if it were unrestricted.

Practical takeaway for the class's own projects: whenever you define a concept, one sentence stating its intended domain (which population, which context, which audience) resolves most domain disputes before they start.

Sources: Gerring, pp. 119–121 (domain). [ILO, Worker cooperatives](https://www.ilo.org/worker-cooperatives) and [Recommendation No. 193, cooperative principles](https://www.ilo.org/resource/other/r193-promotion-cooperatives-recommendation-2002). [OECD, Innovative Citizen Participation and New Democratic Institutions](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/innovative-citizen-participation-and-new-democratic-institutions_339306da-en.html). Member-run association is a hypothetical teaching example.
:::

## Diagnose: affective polarization, stretched

**Partisan meaning:** Positive feelings toward one's own party and negative feelings toward the opposing party or its supporters.

**Then applied to:** Dislike of any other group, without specifying a political divide or an in-group/out-group comparison.

If disliking a rival sports team's fans counts, what distinguishes affective polarization from **general out-group dislike**?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 37–39 minutes.

Now pose a hypothetical extension: a researcher observes that people dislike a different occupational group, a rival sports team's fans, or some unfamiliar social group and calls that “affective polarization.” Ask: “Which attributes of the original concept are still present? Which have disappeared?” If the label now means any negative evaluation of any group, the political or partisan division has been dropped. If only one target group's rating is observed, the comparison underlying the claim may also be unspecified.

Connect this to intension and extension. Relaxing the defining requirements expands the range of cases the term can cover. The conceptual stretching occurs when the researcher retains the same label and imports its interpretation without acknowledging or defending the altered definition. The problem is not that group dislike is unimportant; it is that the label may no longer distinguish this phenomenon from general prejudice, antipathy, or intergroup bias.

Do not present the sports-fan example as an error documented in a particular published study. It is a hypothetical application designed to expose the boundary question. Nor should students infer that every extension beyond political parties is illegitimate. A researcher can develop a broader concept around other political identities or group divisions, but must specify the relevant groups, what makes them opposing camps, the affective comparison, and how the broader concept differs from ordinary group dislike.

Ask: “Are we observing dislike, a division in affect between groups, or an increase in that division over time?” A low rating of one group alone does not establish all three. Keep the definition, its measurement, and claims about change separate. Let students diagnose the problem before naming consistency on the next slide.

Sources: [Iyengar, Sood, and Lelkes (2012), “Affect, Not Ideology”](https://academic.oup.com/poq/article-abstract/76/3/405/1894274), for the partisan formulation. Gerring, pp. 121–123, for consistency and conceptual stretching. Broad group-dislike examples are instructor hypotheticals.
:::

## Criterion 3: Consistency

**Bad:** Moving from partisan affective divisions to any group dislike while treating the meaning as unchanged.

**Good:** Explicitly define and justify a broader concept, specify its groups and comparisons, and distinguish it from general out-group dislike.

::: key-line
Consistency: does the concept mean the same thing throughout a work?
:::

**Revise social media:** Are you applying the same membership rule to every candidate platform?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 39–41 minutes.

There are several defensible responses. Retain the narrower partisan definition and restrict the cases accordingly. Explicitly construct a broader concept of affective divisions across specified groups, explaining its membership requirements and relationship to the partisan version. Or use a label such as out-group dislike when that is all the evidence establishes. A broader definition must supply enough content to distinguish the phenomenon from neighboring concepts; announcing a broader scope is necessary but does not by itself make the definition useful.

Reconnect to intension and extension: removing a defining requirement can enlarge the set of qualifying cases. An explicit redefinition allows readers to evaluate that change. Applying the old label to newly included cases while treating all the old implications as established conceals it.

Return to social media. Suppose the definition requires users to create content and interact with one another. A news website that only allows reading does not meet that definition merely because its articles are shared elsewhere. Either exclude it under the existing rule or revise the rule explicitly and apply it again to every case. This hypothetical transfers the same reasoning to students' working definition.

Source: Gerring, pp. 121–123. Affective polarization and social media are classroom applications; the partisan starting point is Iyengar, Sood, and Lelkes (2012), cited on the preceding slide.
:::

## Diagnose: "the West"

Seven contiguous US states, defined mostly by geography.

What, besides being next to each other, do they share?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 41–43 minutes.

Present "the West" as a US regional concept and ask the class what unifies it besides contiguity. Push for specifics: climate? History of settlement? Political culture? Economic base? Most answers will struggle — precisely Gerring's point. Compare, only after they've struggled, to "the South," which the class will likely find easier to defend: a genuinely longer, more correlated list of shared historical, political, and cultural attributes (a specific settlement and agricultural history, a distinct regional political culture, clear contrasts with neighboring regions).

Do not yet name the criterion. Let the class sit with the asymmetry: both are geographic labels: only one earns its status as a meaningful social-science category.

Source: Gerring, pp. 124–125.
:::

## Criterion 4: Fecundity

**Bad:** "the West" — a merely contiguous set with little else in common; the boundary feels arbitrary.

**Good:** "the South" — a long list of correlated attributes; the label carries real explanatory punch.

::: key-line
Fecundity: how many attributes do a concept's referents actually share?
:::

::: notes
Name the criterion: *fecundity* (also called coherence, depth, richness — Gerring lists many synonyms because this criterion has been independently discovered under many names). A fecund concept "carves nature at the joints" — it identifies things that really are alike and separates them from things that are really different, rather than imposing an arbitrary label on a loose grab-bag.

Make explicit a distinction the diagnosis can blur: "the West" failing fecundity does not mean it isn't a concept. It has a term ("the West"), an intension (located west of some line), an indicator (check a state's location), and an extension (the actual states counted) — every element Gerring requires. It's a fully formed, resonant, class concept; it simply scores low on this one criterion. Contrast with the earlier "furry, four-legged animal" case, which failed at the level of *resonance* — nobody would recognize it as invoking democracy at all. "Is this a concept?" and "is this a *good* concept?" are different questions; the six criteria are all answers to the second one, not the first.

The deepest form of fecundity, per Gerring, is an *essentializing* definition — one that identifies a single core principle from which the concept's other attributes can be seen to follow (Dahl's search for the "primitive notion" behind "power"; "rule by the people" as democracy's essence, which is itself an appeal to fecundity, not just resonance). Ask the class directly: "what is the essential attribute tying the members of 'the West' together, if any?" If nothing beyond location comes back, that silence is the diagnosis. Note for the class: fecundity and resonance are related but distinct — a concept can resonate (match common usage) while still being only weakly fecund (loosely bundled, not very illuminating), and vice versa.

Bridge to the next criterion: Gerring explicitly calls fecundity and differentiation "flip sides of the same coin" — fecundity asks how alike a concept's members are to each other; differentiation asks how different they are from everything outside the concept. You cannot fully assess one without the other.

Social media application (instructor exercise): Ask what knowing that a service is social media lets us infer about it. Sharing an internet connection alone may give a precise but uninformative class. Seek coherent shared characteristics rather than lengthening the definition for its own sake.

Source: Gerring, pp. 123–127.
:::

## Diagnose: an alphabet soup of "civic groups"

Civic association. Voluntary association. Civil society organization (CSO). Citizen sector organization. NGO. Interest group. Grassroots organization.

Seven terms. How many genuinely different concepts?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 45–47 minutes.

List Gerring's own example of a "crowded semantic field" and ask the class to sort it: are these seven terms picking out seven genuinely distinct concepts, or largely re-labeling the same thing? Most will (correctly) suspect heavy overlap. Push further: what's the actual cost of this proliferation, beyond mere redundancy? The cost is that a reader can no longer tell, from the term alone, what distinguishes one from another — each new coinage should in principle sharpen a boundary, but in practice these terms mostly poach attributes from each other without clarifying any of them.

Do not yet name the criterion — let students propose it. Likely candidates: "they're not different enough from each other," "there's no clear boundary between them." Both are gesturing at the right idea.

Source: Gerring, pp. 127–129.
:::

## Criterion 5: Differentiation

**Bad:** seven overlapping civic-group terms with no clear boundaries between them — Gerring's "conceptual anarchy."

**Good:** "contestation" — a single attribute that cleanly separates democracies from autocracies.

::: key-line
Differentiation: what is the contrast-space against which this concept defines itself?
:::

::: notes
Name the criterion: *differentiation* — a concept must be distinguishable from its neighbors, not just internally coherent. "Green" only means something because it's delimited by where "yellow" and "blue" begin (Gerring, citing Pitkin); a new term that "unsettles the semantic field" by poaching attributes from neighbors sows confusion even if it resonates on first reading.

"Contestation" as a defining attribute of democracy earns strong differentiation because it draws a genuinely sharp line against the neighboring concept of autocracy — a polity either does or does not hold meaningfully contested elections, and that single question does real boundary-drawing work. Contrast with the seven civic-group terms, which fail to specify what lies *outside* each of them relative to the others.

Tie explicitly back to fecundity: "apples and oranges" — fecundity asks whether apples cohere as a category; differentiation asks whether apples are cleanly distinguished from oranges. A concept with only one of the two is in trouble either way: coherent-but-undifferentiated collapses into its neighbors, and differentiated-but-incoherent is just an arbitrary boundary around unrelated things.

Social media application (instructor exercise): Test adjacent categories without assuming they must be disjoint. Ask which attribute justifies each distinction and whether overlap should be acknowledged.

Source: Gerring, pp. 127–129.
:::

## What does “social media use” mean in a causal claim?

**Claim:** “Social media use increases political knowledge.”

Two people each spend 30 minutes on social media:

-   One reads explanations of candidates’ policy proposals.
-   One exchanges birthday messages with friends.

Both have the same amount of **social media use**. Have they experienced the same proposed cause?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 49–51 minutes.

If the proposed explanation is that people learn political facts by encountering political information, then the distinction between these activities matters. A total-time measure combines time spent encountering that information with time spent doing something else. Two identical scores therefore need not represent identical exposure to the proposed cause. We have identified a possible mismatch between the causal explanation and the concept used to express and measure it.

Ask: “What would we need to know in addition to the number of minutes?” Expected answers include what content people encountered, whether it contained political information, and whether they attended to it. These answers help specify the relevant cause. Do not claim that birthday messages can never carry political information or that reading a policy explanation necessarily increases knowledge. The examples specify contrasting activities; their effects remain empirical questions.

A more specific hypothesis might be: “Reading accurate explanations of candidates' policy proposals on social media increases knowledge of those proposals.” The researcher would still need to specify the comparison, observation period, and measurement of knowledge. The point is not to prove the narrower claim; it is to state a cause that fits the proposed explanation well enough to investigate it.

A broad concept is not automatically wrong. If the question were about the effect of access to an entire platform, its combination of activities could be exactly what the researcher wants to study. For example, a comparison of access versus no access would address a different question from a comparison of political versus nonpolitical content. Choose the concept in relation to the question rather than assume narrower is always better.

Source: Instructor social media illustration of Gerring's causal-utility criterion, pp. 130–131. These are hypothetical activities and causal claims, not reported findings.
:::

## Criterion 6: Causal utility

**Does the concept help us state and investigate the causal question?**

**Question:** Does encountering political information on social media help people learn about candidates?

**Too broad for that explanation:** Total time on social media combines political information with many other activities.

::: notes
**Outcome:** Knowledge of those policies, assessed separately from exposure.

Translate “causal utility” as “usefulness for the causal question.” Gerring's point is that a concept must do more than describe a recognizable category. When it enters a causal argument, its definition should help us identify what is supposed to make a difference and what difference we are trying to explain.

Work through the example in three steps. First, identify the proposed cause: encountering accurate information about candidates' policy proposals. Second, identify the comparison: encountering nonpolitical content instead. Third, identify the outcome: knowledge of those policy proposals. Each term needs a definition that allows it to be distinguished and observed. The concept “social media use” alone does not specify this contrast because both activities qualify as social media use.

Make the research example concrete. Imagine randomly assigning participants to spend the same amount of time reading either a specified set of accurate policy explanations or a specified set of nonpolitical posts in a social media setting. Assess policy knowledge with questions scored for accuracy. This would test the effect of those content conditions in that setting, not the effect of all social media use everywhere. Random assignment concerns how we identify an effect; defining the conditions concerns what effect we are trying to identify. The latter is the conceptual issue on this slide.

Explain why the outcome must be separate. Do not define “informative exposure” as “exposure that made someone more knowledgeable” and then announce that informative exposure increases knowledge. That would build the outcome into the definition of the cause. Identify the content independently of participants' responses, then measure whether knowledge differs. A participant who learns nothing must still count as having received the assigned information.

The broad category remains useful for other purposes, such as describing where people spend time. It can also serve a broad causal question about access to a platform as a whole. The issue is fit: a category that works for one question may combine distinctions that another question needs to preserve. A well-defined broad intervention can have causal utility, and a narrowly named variable can still be poorly defined.

End by asking students to complete: “For my question, the relevant aspect of social media is ***; I would compare*** with ***; the outcome is*** .” Then ask which activities their narrower concept excludes and why that exclusion serves their question. Their answer should identify the proposed cause independently of its hoped-for effect.

Source: Gerring, pp. 130–131, on concepts in causal arguments, specifying treatments, and distinguishing causes from effects. Social media example and hypothetical experiment are instructor applications.
:::


## Two answers to "how do you actually build one?" {.section-title}

Gerring: **survey → classify attributes → define** (minimal / maximal / cumulative).

McLeod & Pan: **Chaffee's six steps** of concept explication.

::: key-line
Same underlying logic, developed independently in two different literatures.
:::

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 58–61 minutes.

Reorient after the break. The six criteria just covered tell you whether a finished concept is *good*. This segment covers how you actually *arrive* at one — and two readings converge on strikingly similar answers, which is itself worth pointing out explicitly as evidence that this isn't idiosyncratic to either author.

Preview both lists on the board side by side so the alignment is visible from the start:

Gerring's three-step Strategies of Conceptualization: (1) *survey* plausible concepts and existing usages broadly, resisting "premature closure"; (2) *classify attributes* into a single table, distilling many overlapping definitions into a parsimonious lexical map; (3) *define*, choosing among minimal, maximal, or cumulative strategies.

Chaffee's six-step concept explication (via McLeod & Pan): (1) identify the concept; (2) search the literature; (3) examine empirical properties; (4) develop a tentative conceptual definition; (5) define the concept operationally; (6) gather data.

Tell the class we'll work through both using Gerring's own running example (democracy) for steps 1–3 of his framework, then re-run the *identical* logic on a live, current example — Molina et al.'s explication of "fake news" — for the rest of class.

Source: Gerring, pp. 131–137; McLeod & Pan, pp. 26–28.
:::

## Step 1–3 aligned: survey, classify, and search the literature

| Gerring | McLeod & Pan (Chaffee) |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Survey** plausible concepts and usages | **Search the literature** |
| **Classify attributes** into one table | **Examine empirical properties** |
| *(next: define)* | **Identify the concept** *(comes first, but same spirit: what exactly is this?)* |

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 61–64 minutes.

Walk the table left to right, one row at a time, making the equivalence explicit rather than just implied. Gerring's *survey* step (canvass a representative sample of formal definitions and usage patterns before committing to one) is functionally identical to Chaffee's *search the literature* step (review how previous researchers have conceptualized the topic, what purposes each served, what labels have been used). Both are explicitly a caution against jumping straight to a definition.

Gerring's *classify attributes* step (reduce the many overlapping usages into one parsimonious table — his own worked example, Table 5.3, sorts democracy's attributes into six families: electoral, liberal, majoritarian, participatory, deliberative, egalitarian) matches Chaffee's *examine empirical properties* step (what's the range and distribution of how this concept has actually been measured and used).

Note the one place they diverge in sequencing rather than substance: Chaffee puts *identify the concept* — is this even one variable, what's the unit of analysis, what purpose does it serve — as step 1, before the literature search, while Gerring treats "what is this concept, really" as something the survey itself helps answer. Tell the class not to worry about the exact ordering; both authors explicitly say their steps aren't always taken in the listed order. What matters is that all of survey/classify/identify happen *before* committing to a definition — exactly the discipline the "social media is harmful" mega-concept lacked.

Source: Gerring, pp. 131–134; McLeod & Pan, p. 26.
:::

## Step 4, the real choice: minimal, maximal, or cumulative

**Minimal** — necessary conditions only: democracy = free & fair elections. Crisp borders.

**Maximal** — every non-idiosyncratic attribute, ideal-type. Rich, but a matter of degree.

**Cumulative** — attributes ranked by centrality into an ordinal scale.

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 64–66 minutes.

This is Gerring's Table 5.2, and it is the direct payoff of the causal-utility slide from before the break — say so explicitly. *Minimal* definitions (necessary conditions, jointly sufficient to bound the concept, aiming for crisp in/out borders) are what we already saw work well as a scope condition or independent variable; the cost is some loss of resonance, since a stripped-down definition sounds thin to anyone attuned to the concept's usual richness.

*Maximal* definitions (Weber's "ideal-type": synthesizing many diffuse, real-world cases into one purest, most fully elaborated analytical construct) bundle in everything non-idiosyncratic; no actual case need fit perfectly, and cases are scored by degree of resemblance. This is exactly the tool that failed as a scope condition earlier, and exactly the tool Gerring says fits a rich dependent variable well.

*Cumulative* definitions try to split the difference: rank the attributes by how essential each is to the concept and use the count of satisfied attributes as an ordinal scale. This buys some of maximal's degree-sensitivity while keeping minimal's crisp, binary attributes; the cost is that you can't presume equal spacing between levels (an ordinal, not interval, scale).

Tell the class we're about to see exactly what a maximal definition and a cumulative definition look like, worked out in full for democracy — the next two slides show Gerring's own Tables 5.3 and 5.4.

Source: Gerring, pp. 134–137, Table 5.2.
:::

## Democracy’s attributes: the starting point for a definition

![](assets/gerring-table5.3-democracy-attributes.png){fig-alt="Gerring's Table 5.3: a classification of fundamental attributes of democracy, organized into six families — Electoral, Liberal, Majoritarian, Participatory, Deliberative, and Egalitarian — each with its own principles, guiding question, and institutions, all under the shared core principle of rule by the people."}

::: project-caption
Gerring, Table 5.3 (p. 135) .
:::

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 66–69 minutes.

Show Gerring's own lexical classification of democracy's attributes in full — this is literally what "classify attributes" (step 2 of Strategies of Conceptualization) produces before any minimal/maximal/cumulative choice gets made. Six families, each with its own principle, guiding question, and institutional markers: Electoral (contestation — free and fair multiparty elections), Liberal (limited government, civil liberties, horizontal accountability), Majoritarian (majority rule, centralization), Participatory (do ordinary citizens participate?), Deliberative (government by reason), Egalitarian (political equality). All six share one core principle: rule by the people — the resonance anchor from Criterion 1.

Walk through why this table, on its own, "does not take us very far toward a final definition," in Gerring's own words: it's comprehensive but unwieldy — eighteen-plus institutional markers across six families is not something you can cleanly apply to sort real countries into democracies and non-democracies. This is exactly the tension fecundity (rich, comprehensive) creates with causal utility (needs crisp borders) — a maximal, ideal-type definition of democracy is literally what you get if you keep this entire table intact as the definition, scoring each polity by degree of resemblance across all six families rather than picking one attribute as necessary.

Ask the class: "if we were using this as a *dependent* variable — something we're trying to explain the full richness of — is keeping all six families a problem?" Generally no; this is exactly the case (Criterion 6) where a maximal definition is the right tool.

Unpack how a maximal definition actually gets scored, since "degree of resemblance" is easy to say and easy to leave vague. Gerring's own answer: ideal-types are "always matters of degree, and hence generally operationalized by interval scales" — so a country isn't sorted into democracy/not-democracy, it's placed somewhere along a continuous scale representing how closely it approximates the full six-family bundle. Flag honestly that this chapter tells us *that* it's scored by degree, not *how* to combine eighteen-plus institutional markers into one number — Gerring explicitly defers the mechanics of building that scale to Chapter 6 (measurement).

That deferral is itself the first problem worth naming. Five distinct costs of a maximal definition, beyond the causal-utility point already made:

1. **No stated aggregation rule.** Nothing here says how to weight or combine the six families — average them? weight electoral more heavily than deliberative? Different reasonable choices can rank the same set of countries differently, and the maximal-definition logic itself doesn't adjudicate between them.
2. **No crisp cutoff, by design.** Because everything is a matter of degree, there's no natural line separating "democracy" from "not" — fine for a rich descriptive/dependent variable, but exactly why it fails as a scope condition or independent variable.
3. **Attribute redundancy.** Many of the eighteen-plus markers across families tend to co-occur historically (strong electoral competition often travels with stronger civil liberties), so a naive additive score risks counting substantially the same underlying dimension more than once rather than genuinely independent information.
4. **Researcher discretion masquerading as neutrality.** Because weighting is undetermined, two researchers can build "the same" ideal-type democracy score and rank countries differently depending on which families they emphasize — the identical mega-concept problem as the Druckman & Levendusky affective-polarization example from earlier: one label, several non-interchangeable operationalizations.
5. **Unfalsifiability at the edges.** No case needs to fit perfectly, which is a feature for capturing richness but also means the definition alone can never rule anything out — any country can be described as "partially" resembling the ideal type.

Transition: "Now watch what happens when we go the other direction — ranking, not bundling."

Source: Gerring, Table 5.3, p. 135, and p. 136 on ideal-types and interval scales.
:::

## The cumulative ordinal scale: Table 5.4

![](assets/gerring-table5.4-cumulative-democracy.png){fig-alt="Gerring's Table 5.4: a cumulative definition of democracy as a nine-point ordinal scale, where attribute (a) free and fair elections is required at every level, and successive levels 2 through 9 each add one more attribute in descending order of centrality: self-government domestic, self-government complete, executive elected and paramount, universal male suffrage, universal suffrage, executive constitutionality, executive constraints, and civil liberty."}

::: project-caption
Gerring, Table 5.4 (p. 138).
:::

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 69–72 minutes.

Show the cumulative scale in full. Read the logic of the x's directly off the table: level 1 requires only free and fair elections; level 2 requires that plus self-government (domestic); level 3 adds complete self-government; and so on up through level 9, which requires all nine attributes including civil liberty. Every polity that qualifies at level 9 also qualifies at every lower level — that's what makes it cumulative (a Guttman-scale-like structure, Gerring notes, but ranking theoretical attributes rather than empirical indicators).

Make the double payoff explicit. First, notice attribute (a) is exactly the minimal definition from three slides ago — cumulative doesn't discard minimal, it starts from it and builds outward. Second, point out — as Gerring himself flags — that not all of Table 5.3's lexical attributes made it into this cumulative scale (nothing here directly represents "deliberative" or full "egalitarian" empowerment, for instance): ranking attributes by centrality is itself a judgment call, and this table reflects one defensible ranking, not the only possible one.

Ask the class: "what do we gain by using this cumulative scale instead of just the six-family maximal table?" Expected answer: a single ordinal number per country (how many attributes it satisfies) that lets you *order* all polities by degree of democracy — solving what Gerring calls the aggregation problem — while still keeping each individual attribute a crisp yes/no. What we lose: we can't say a level-6 country is "twice as democratic" as a level-3 country — only that it ranks higher, since the levels aren't guaranteed to be equally spaced (ordinal, not interval).

Source: Gerring, Table 5.4, p. 138.
:::

## Social media: which definition strategy fits?

1.  **Minimal:** Which attributes are necessary, and together sufficient, for a service to count?
2.  **Maximal:** What additional attributes describe an ideal type?
3.  **Cumulative:** Can you defend an ordering of attributes by centrality?

Which approach fits classifying platforms? Which fits comparing their characteristics?

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 72–74 minutes.

Return to the running example one more time and make the class apply the new vocabulary to it directly, cold-call, whole class. A minimal definition might be a single necessary condition: willingness to let a disliked group hold a public meeting (exactly the operationalization Week 2 actually used). A maximal, ideal-type definition would bundle in absence of hostile feeling, public and private consistency, durability over time, and generalization across multiple disliked groups — a much richer construct, but one where few real respondents would perfectly qualify.

For a cumulative definition, ask whether there is a defensible ordering of binary attributes from more to less essential. A checklist or weighted sum is not automatically a cumulative definition. It is acceptable to conclude that these attributes do not form a convincing cumulative hierarchy.

Tie the choice to the research purpose. A minimal rule can delimit the population of platforms. An ideal type can describe degrees of resemblance. Neither, by itself, specifies a person's exposure or activity as a causal variable.

Source: Instructor application of Gerring, pp. 135–138.
:::

## Levels of abstraction: what counts as social media?

| Abstraction level | Term | Social media example |
|---|---|---|
| **High** | Concept (construct) | Social media |
| **Intermediate** | Dimensions | User content creation · Interaction among users · Connections among users |
| **Low (concrete)** | Indicators | Publishing text, images, or video for others to see · Replying to another user or holding a conversation · Following accounts, adding contacts, or joining groups |

**Your turn:** Which attributes does your definition require? Would a news website with comments qualify?

::: project-caption
Classroom application of McLeod & Pan’s levels of abstraction (pp. 29–31), following the structure of their Figure 2.1. Proposed attributes, not a settled definition.
:::

::: notes
Read the table's left-hand column aloud first: **ABSTRACTION LEVEL** — High, Intermediate, Low (concrete) — mapped onto **TERMS** — Concept (construct), Dimensions, Indicators. This is McLeod & Pan's Figure 2.1 structure, applied live to our own running example instead of their television-viewing case. It's the explicit vocabulary for something we've been doing all class without naming it: every time we've moved from a mega-concept to something measurable, we've been moving *down* a level of abstraction, and every time we've bundled specifics back into one label, we've moved *up* one.

Walk the table top to bottom. High abstraction: "social media" as a single concept/construct — abstract enough to apply across many platforms, times, and studies, per the abstractness standard from earlier, but, as we diagnosed a few slides ago, too abstract to relate cleanly to most effect variables on its own. Intermediate abstraction: the three dimensions on the board — content creation, interaction, connections — still abstract (each is its own variable concept, not yet a specific observation), but narrower and closer to something we could actually code. Low, concrete abstraction: the indicators — specific, directly observable yes/no questions about a given platform.

Use the "your turn" prompt to make the ladder do real work, not just get labeled. Take a news website with a comment section: it likely satisfies the *interaction* dimension (readers can reply to each other) but not *connections* (no following, no contact lists) and only weakly *content creation* (comments, not full posts). Whether it counts as "social media" then depends entirely on which dimensions the class's working definition treats as necessary versus optional — precisely the minimal/maximal/cumulative choice from two slides ago, now visible as a concrete borderline case rather than an abstract choice.

Make the general point explicit, not just about social media: *any* concept can be placed somewhere on this same High/Intermediate/Low ladder, and explication is largely the discipline of being honest about which level you're currently operating at. "Fake news" (coming up shortly) is a High-abstraction mega-concept exactly like "social media"; its eight categories are Intermediate-level dimensions; its Table 1 indicators (fact-checked, last-name citations, editorial process) are Low-level, concrete, and directly codable — we will explicitly walk back up and down this same three-level ladder when we get there.

Flag why dimensionalizing (moving down one level, from High to Intermediate) matters theoretically, not just practically, using McLeod & Pan's own finding: they report that news viewing and entertainment viewing — two dimensions of "television viewing," their running example — relate to political-knowledge and crime-fear outcomes in *opposite* directions, a finding invisible if "television viewing" were left undifferentiated at the High level. The same risk applies here: if "social media use" is left as one undifferentiated High-level variable, dimensions that move outcomes in opposite directions (say, following news accounts versus scrolling an algorithmic entertainment feed) could cancel each other out in the data.

Note the vocabulary McLeod & Pan use for concepts built this way: *constructs* — concepts intentionally built with specially defined meanings (via explicit dimensions) rather than borrowed from everyday usage. Concept and construct are treated as equivalent for our purposes.

Source: Instructor application of McLeod & Pan, pp. 29–31, Figure 2.1. The social media dimensions, indicators, and observations are classroom proposals, not a validated taxonomy or measurement instrument.
:::

## Social media: from definition to cases

| Task | Apply it to the same concept |
|---|---|
| **Specify the intension** | Which platform attributes define social media? |
| **State the membership rule** | Which attributes are required, and in what combination? |
| **Identify indicators** | What observations tell us whether each attribute is present? |
| **Determine the extension** | Which platforms meet the rule? Which do not? |

**Check:** Can another researcher apply your definition to an unfamiliar platform?

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 79–82 minutes.

Connect the readings without equating their frameworks. Gerring's definition strategies concern the selection and organization of attributes. McLeod & Pan's levels of abstraction help us articulate the concept's aspects and connect them to observations. A minimal definition is not simply one dimension, and a list of indicators is not automatically a cumulative scale.

Flag the ordering and a distinction the table makes look cleaner than it strictly is. The order runs left to right for a reason: an intension has to exist before you can state a membership rule over it; the rule is worth settling before hunting for indicators, because it determines which attributes actually need one (minimal only strictly needs indicators for the necessary attributes; maximal needs them for everything); and extension comes last because it's the output — apply the indicators to real platforms, apply the rule, see who qualifies.

But be honest that "specify the intension" and "state the membership rule" are not two separate elements in Gerring's own vocabulary — they're one. A fully specified intension isn't just a list of attributes; it already includes how those attributes are understood to combine (necessary, sufficient, or additive-and-continuous — the same logic from the Figure 5.1 tradeoff). The table splits this into two rows for a didactic reason, not a technical one: it's exactly the gap the seven weak everyday approaches diagnosed earlier — defining by examples, by exclusion, or by comparing subsets all hand you attributes or cases without ever stating how they combine into a rule. Separating "list the attributes" from "state how they combine" turns that common silent failure into an explicit, checkable step. Tell the class directly: Gerring has four elements, not five; this is a decomposition of one of them.

Work through the same borderline platform using the stated rule. If students disagree, locate the disagreement: intended meaning, the membership rule, or evidence about the platform. Those are different problems and call for different revisions. Keep an unresolved case open if the necessary evidence is unavailable.

A proposed attribute belongs to the intension; an observation supplies evidence about it; a qualifying platform belongs to the extension. The goal is to connect these levels clearly enough that another researcher can apply the definition. No shift to an individual-level behavior is needed to demonstrate this process.

Source: Instructor synthesis of Gerring, p. 116 and pp. 135–138, and McLeod & Pan, pp. 26–31. Social media is the continuing classroom application.
:::

## "Fake news" is a mega-concept, and it's costing us {.section-title}

Weaponized across the political spectrum. Applied to satire, propaganda, honest mistakes, and outright fabrication alike.

Is "fake news" simply "false information"?

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 82–85 minutes.

Introduce Molina, Sundar, Le & Lee (2019) by first re-diagnosing "fake news" exactly the way we diagnosed "television is harmful" at the start of class — the parallel should feel deliberate and obvious to the class by now. "Fake news" has ballooned, in real political discourse, well beyond any single stable meaning: it gets applied to deliberately fabricated stories, to satire the audience is expected to recognize as such, to honest reporting errors, to strongly one-sided-but-true partisan framing, and, increasingly, as a rhetorical weapon partisans use to dismiss any claim from an opposing side regardless of its truth value.

Ask the class directly: "if a news outlet were trying to build an automated fake-news detector, why would it be a mistake to simply operationalize 'fake news' as 'false information'?" Let a few answers surface before the next slide supplies the paper's own reasoning: false information alone doesn't distinguish a deliberate fabrication from an honest correction, doesn't distinguish propaganda from satire, and gives a machine-learning classifier no way to separate categories that call for very different responses (labeling, fact-checking, no action at all).

Source: Molina et al. (2019), pp. 180–182.
:::

## A serious prior attempt: two dimensions

**Tandoc, Lim & Ling (2018):** classify content by **facticity** (how true is it?) and **intent to deceive** (is deception the goal?).

Propaganda: high facticity risk, high deceptive intent. Fabrication: low facticity, high intent. Satire: high facticity, low intent.

Why isn't this enough?

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 85–88 minutes.

Present Tandoc et al.'s prior typology respectfully, as real, useful scholarship — not a straw man. Placing content on two dimensions, facticity and intent to deceive, is itself a legitimate application of the "classify attributes" step: it takes a mega-concept and identifies at least two real, distinct dimensions bundled inside it, exactly the McLeod & Pan move from two slides ago.

Then present Molina et al.'s own stated objection, which is a genuine methodological point, not a dismissal: facticity is useful for fact-checking established claims, but breaks down for breaking news about emergent events where no independent verification yet exists to check against. Intent to deceive might in principle be inferred from a source's track record, but is very difficult to establish in any single case in a way precise enough to feed a machine-learning algorithm — "intent" is exactly the kind of latent, hard-to-observe construct McLeod & Pan warned resists direct operationalization.

Land the point: Molina et al. are not saying Tandoc et al. were wrong to dimensionalize "fake news" — they're saying two dimensions, while real, were not *specific* enough for their particular purpose (automated detection), which needed a full explication all the way down to concrete, machine-readable indicators. This is the same "does the definition fit its intended use" logic as causal utility, applied to a measurement rather than a causal-inference purpose.

Source: Molina et al. (2019), pp. 182–183, citing Tandoc, Lim, and Ling (2018).
:::

## Chaffee's step 1, enacted: is "fake news" even one variable?

Molina et al.'s answer: **no.** It's at least eight distinct categories, not one true/false binary.

Real news · False news · Polarized content · Satire · Misreporting · Commentary · Persuasive information · Citizen journalism

::: notes
Timing: 3 minutes. Elapsed: 88–91 minutes.

Show the paper's own resolution to "identify the concept" (Chaffee's step 1): rather than trying to force "fake news" into one binary variable (true/false) or even Tandoc et al.'s two continuous dimensions, Molina et al. conclude the concept genuinely decomposes into eight qualitatively distinct categories, organized as a taxonomy rather than a single scale.

Connect this explicitly to earlier material in two directions. First, to McLeod & Pan's dimensions/indicators ladder: this taxonomy is what happens when "dimensionalizing" a mega-concept produces categories rather than continuous dimensions — a legitimate variant of the same underlying move. Second, to Gerring's minimal/maximal/cumulative choice: ask the class to predict, before the next slides confirm it, whether the paper's definition of any *one* category (say, real news) is likely to be minimal, maximal, or cumulative, given that the whole point is a sharp, machine-usable classifier. (Answer, confirmed on the next slides: minimal — necessary-condition attributes, crisp borders, exactly the causal-utility logic, now applied to a classification rather than a causal-inference task.)

State the paper's own stakes plainly: getting this categorization right isn't academic hairsplitting — the paper argues that bluntly labeling any partisan-but-true content "false" in a blanket way can itself backfire, breeding reactance among readers whose politically congenial content gets over-flagged.

Source: Molina et al. (2019), pp. 183, 186–187.
:::

## Chaffee's step 2, enacted: searching the literature

Southwell, Thorson & Sheble (2017): misinformation needs a **grounding of truth**.

Lazer et al. (2018): process and **intent** matter, not just content.

Jack (2017): disentangles propaganda, disinformation, and neighboring concepts.

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes. Elapsed: 91–93 minutes.
